reviews.review:
Thomaz is a compact indie adventure built around an intentionally familiar fantasy premise. You play as Mike, an adventurer who sets out to rescue a princess kidnapped by a demonic wizard after previous rescuers have apparently failed. Rather than surrounding this objective with lengthy cinematics or complicated lore, the game uses the story as a straightforward reason to push through a succession of increasingly challenging stages. Developed and published by Eckalon, it embraces the simplicity of older arcade adventures, concentrating on navigation, hazards, enemies, and reaching the objective rather than trying to deliver a sprawling narrative experience.

The main adventure contains more than 20 levels and gradually increases the difficulty as Mike moves closer to his ultimate confrontation. Level progression incorporates maze-like layouts alongside platforming and action elements, giving players environments that require more than simply moving from one side of the screen to the other. Its mechanics remain relatively uncomplicated, making the fundamentals accessible without demanding mastery of an elaborate collection of abilities. The disadvantage is that players accustomed to modern platformers may eventually find the limited mechanical variety repetitive. There are only a handful of distinct enemy types, so later challenges rely heavily on placement, environmental layouts, and increased pressure rather than constantly introducing new opponents.

The retro presentation complements this uncomplicated approach. Pixel-based graphics and minimalist environments give Thomaz the appearance of an intentionally old-school production rather than a game attempting graphical realism. Medieval and demonic imagery supports the fantasy setting, while the maze-oriented stage construction helps distinguish the environments from conventional linear platforming courses. The visuals are functional more than spectacular, but that is consistent with the project's overall identity. Various improvements made to the game over time have also addressed elements such as menus, dialogs, achievement artwork, widescreen presentation, and general gameplay polish.

A particularly unusual feature is the secondary beet-collecting activity. Instead of restricting players entirely to Mike's rescue mission, the game provides another mode centered on gathering beets. This portion also introduces cooperative play for two players, creating a small multiplayer diversion alongside the predominantly single-player adventure. Remote Play Together support makes the cooperative component more convenient. It is not extensive enough to make multiplayer the central attraction, but it adds welcome variety and gives players something different to try when they want a break from progressing through the main stages.

Achievements are arguably Thomaz's most conspicuous feature. The game contains an exceptionally large collection of Steam achievements, far beyond what would normally be expected from an indie adventure of this size. Achievement presentation has also been expanded and improved, including numerous visual variations involving letters, numbers, fonts, colors, and symbols. For dedicated achievement collectors, this aspect can substantially increase the game's appeal and provide additional goals beyond simply finishing the adventure. For everyone else, the enormous achievement count can feel disproportionate to the depth of the actual gameplay and should be viewed as a bonus rather than evidence of an equally enormous amount of unique content.

The narrative remains deliberately uncomplicated throughout. The kidnapped-princess scenario provides immediate motivation and fits the game's retro sensibilities, but anyone expecting extensive characterization, branching conversations, cinematic storytelling, or elaborate world-building should temper expectations. The emphasis is clearly on progressing through stages and overcoming obstacles. In that respect, the simplicity works reasonably well because players are rarely prevented from getting back to the action by excessive exposition. The trade-off is that the characters and setting have relatively little opportunity to develop beyond their functional roles within the adventure.

Several Steam features help make the package more convenient. Steam Cloud support is useful for preserving progress, while partial controller support provides an alternative input method. Family Sharing is also supported. These conveniences do not fundamentally alter the experience, but they make a small indie production easier to approach across different setups.

Steam Deck compatibility is less straightforward. Thomaz does not have an official Steam Deck Verified or Playable classification displayed for the game, so its compatibility should be regarded as officially unverified rather than guaranteed. The relatively modest nature of the game suggests that it is not especially demanding, but the absence of an official Deck rating means players should not assume that every aspect, including controls, interface behavior, or display presentation, will work perfectly without adjustment. Anyone purchasing specifically for Steam Deck should therefore treat handheld support as uncertain.

Thomaz works best when approached with expectations appropriate to its scale. Its strengths come from accessible arcade-style progression, retro presentation, maze-inspired stages, escalating difficulty, a quirky cooperative beet-collecting diversion, and an extraordinary emphasis on achievements. Its weaknesses are similarly apparent: limited enemy variety, modest mechanical depth, simple storytelling, and the possibility of repetition across the campaign. Players looking for sophisticated combat or an expansive platforming adventure are unlikely to find enough depth here, but those who appreciate straightforward indie games may enjoy its deliberately uncomplicated design.

Ultimately, Thomaz is a modest adventure with a surprisingly eccentric collection of extras surrounding a very traditional core. The rescue mission gives it an immediately understandable objective, while the secondary mode and unusually extensive achievement system provide additional reasons to spend time with it. It does not reinvent its genre and its limited scope prevents it from becoming especially memorable mechanically, yet it possesses enough personality to distinguish itself among small retro-inspired releases. For achievement hunters and players who enjoy simple arcade adventures, it has considerably more appeal than its basic premise might initially suggest.

Rating: 6/10
